text: Ἐπινοητικὴν οἶδε τὴν νοερὰν τῆς ψυχῆς δύναμιν. Expositio est ejus quod dixerat superiori, c. 100 τὴν τῶν ἡδέων ἐπινοητικὴν σχέσιν: sic passim, aliam alia sententia Maximus exponit, ac si esset diversus auctor. Esseque non raro suadeat Photii ipsa censura, a limine Quæst. ad Thalassium posita, et quod ipse quandoque deprehendi, Marci quædam αὐτολεξεὶ inserta aliis Maximi Capita. Refert ergo illud, οἶδε, superiorem auctorem, qui sic intellectum aut rationem, facultatem animi ἐπινοητικὴν (id est, excogitandi seu inveniendi solertem) quasi paraphrasi vocaverit, non divinam Scripturam aut sermonem, ut non bene reddidit Picus. Socus cum additur λόγος, uti quandoque facit Maximus, ac passim alii theologi.
anchorLine: ναμιν (l)· ἥτις χωριζομένη τῆς κατ᾽ αἴσθησιν σχέ-
en: "Ἐπινοητικὴν οἶδε τὴν νοερὰν τῆς ψυχῆς δύναμιν." This explains what he said earlier, in ch. 100, "τὴν τῶν ἡδέων ἐπινοητικὴν σχέσιν"; so throughout, Maximus explains one opinion by another, as if he were a different author. Photius's own censure, set at the head of the Questions to Thalassius, often suggests this, and I have myself sometimes found some passages of Mark inserted word for word into other Chapters of Maximus. So the word "οἶδε" refers back to the earlier author, who thus called the intellect or reason, the faculty of the soul, ἐπινοητική (that is, skilled at devising or inventing), as if by paraphrase, not the divine Scripture or a saying, as Picus did not render it well. [Printed 'Socus'] when λόγος is added, as Maximus sometimes does, and as other theologians generally do.

text: Ὁ ἀπαθῶς τὰ θεῖα ζητῶν. Nempe sedatum animum petit oratio ac illibatum : quidquid denique ea vox, toties hic Maximo inculcata, Græcorum usu insinuat. Erant edita male luxata, confusis hoc et sequenti capite ; nonnullis etiam desideratis. Importune Picus, dicta de Verbo in carne, quasi de nobis ac de carne ipsa, dicta reddit.
anchorLine: ιεʹ. Ὁ ἀπαθῶς τὰ θεῖα ζητῶν (m), πάντως λήψεται,
en: "Ὁ ἀπαθῶς τὰ θεῖα ζητῶν" (he who seeks divine things without passion). Prayer, that is, seeks a calm and untroubled mind, whatever that word, so often stressed here by Maximus, implies in Greek usage. The printed editions were badly dislocated, this chapter and the next being confused, and some things left out. Picus, inappropriately, renders what is said of the Word in the flesh as if it were said of us and of the flesh itself.

text: Ἡ ἄρρητος περιχώρησις τοῦ πεπιστευμένου. Alia profano usu hujus vocis significatio, quam hic conveniat. Quod vero reddit Picus, arcana processio, non satisfacit; nec satis video quid ea voce velit. Budæus longe doctior in Damasceno de Trinit. divinam personarum περιχώρησιν, unionem reddit; quod forte paulo liberius est : theologi circumincessionem vocant, quasi unius personæ in aliam undique immeationem; malim ego, quod una capiat aliam ac velut contineat et comprehendat; quomodo etiam dicuntur divinæ personæ ἀνεκφοιτήτως procedere, ita ut alia extra aliam non excedant : quæ vocis χωρεῖν, trita admodum significatio est, soletque et ad animum transferri, quod ille quasi continendo ac in se rem habendo, intelligat. Sic ergo Maximum intelligo. Manifestationem ac revelationem rei creditæ ac Dei (quæ fit per dona Spiritus adjuvantia fidem) ejus in nobis comprehensionem esse ac perceptionem : ut hinc in nobis habitantem habeamus ipsumque præsentem ac nobis intimum cognoscamus, juxta illud Pauli (Ephes. iii, 17) : Habitare Christum per fidem in cordibus vestris. Nec istud vetat aliquid arcanam unionem dicere, et quasi commistionem, juxta quod Hesych. περιχωρεῖ, συμμίγεται exponit. Sed in his balbutimus, etsi Græci paulo nobis vocibus sunt feliciores. In aliis, nihil fere Picus felicior, ut quod ἀεικίνητος στάσις, illi est, conditio semper movens ; non quia jugi incitata motu ; qualis fruentium Deo.
anchorLine: ἐκάστῳ πίστεως ἄρρητος τοῦ πεπιστευμένου (n)
en: "Ἡ ἄρρητος περιχώρησις τοῦ πεπιστευμένου" (the ineffable interpenetration of what is believed). The word has another sense in profane usage than the one that fits here. Picus's rendering, 'arcana processio' (hidden procession), does not satisfy, and I do not quite see what he means by the word. Budaeus, far more learned, in the Damascene on the Trinity renders the divine persons' perichoresis as 'union', which is perhaps a little loose; theologians call it circumincession, as if one person's passing into another on every side; I would prefer 'that one takes in the other and as it were contains and comprehends it', as the divine persons are also said to proceed inseparably (anekphoitos), so that one does not go outside the other: the verb chorein has a very common meaning and is also used of the mind, which understands by containing and holding the thing in itself. So I understand Maximus thus: the manifestation and revelation of the thing believed and of God (which comes about through the gifts of the Spirit that aid faith) is our comprehension and perception of him, so that we have him dwelling in us and know him present and most intimate to us, according to Paul (Eph. iii, 17): 'that Christ dwell by faith in your hearts.' Nor does this forbid calling it a hidden union and as it were a commingling, as Hesychius explains perichorei as 'is mingled'. But in these matters we stammer, though the Greeks are somewhat better off than we in vocabulary. Elsewhere Picus is hardly happier, as when he renders 'aeikinetos stasis' as 'a condition ever moving', and not as a stability driven by perpetual motion, such as that of those who enjoy God.

text: Τὴν μὲν σχετικήν. Nulla hic commodius voce reddi videatur, quam si intentionalem dicamus; quasi in animi rationibus et apprehensione positam; quam et abstractivam rudiori vocabulo nostri theologi vocant. Affinis usus illius vocis Patribus vii synodi, dum adorationem imaginum, quam sanciunt, σχετικήν vocant; quæ scilicet non ad ipsam rem, ut in se est, terminatur, sed ut in sui similitudine, animo cogitanti quasi præsens objicitur, ac quadam in eam intentione ac motu, secundum quam dicitur honor imaginis transire ad exemp'ar seu prototypum. Nihil ad rem, quod Picus semel et iterum reconditam. Ac certe longe inauditum mundo, quod quis ex ejus interpretamentis conficeret vocabularium: sic sine judicio cuncta viro arbitraria; ut quod hic, ἡ μεθέξει κατ᾽ ἐνέργειαν γνῶσις, illi cognitio est particeps operationis: quod ἔφεσιν, pro αἴσθησιν decoquit, etc.
anchorLine: τὴν μέν, σχετικὴν (o), ὡς ἐν λόγῳ μόνῳ κειμένην
en: "Τὴν μὲν σχετικήν" (the relational one). No word seems to render it better here than 'intentional', as if lodged in the soul's reckonings and apprehension; our theologians also call it, in a cruder term, 'abstractive'. The Fathers of the seventh council use the word in a kindred way when they call the veneration of images that they sanction 'relational': it does not terminate in the thing itself as it is in itself, but is set before the thinking mind as if present in its likeness, with a certain intention and movement toward it, according to which the honor of the image is said to pass to the exemplar or prototype. Picus's 'reconditam' (hidden), repeated again and again, is beside the point. And it is certainly unheard of anywhere that someone should compile a vocabulary from his renderings: so everything becomes arbitrary to the man without judgment; as here, where the Greek 'ἡ μεθέξει κατ᾽ ἐνέργειαν γνῶσις' becomes in him 'knowledge that is a partaker of operation', and 'ἔφεσιν' he boils down to 'αἴσθησιν', and so on.

text: Ἀναιτίως προηγήσατο τῆς γενέσεως. Quod semel et iterum cavet Maximus, hoc et 39 cap. ne τὸ ἀναιτίως et ἀναίτιον, quasi innoxium et sine culpa accipiatur, quæ est proclivis ejus vocis acceptio, id vero propense Picus amplectitur, ac ubique interpretatur. Est certe hæc voluptas eo sensu haud ἀναίτιος, sed culpæ conjuncta, et ex culpa, ni magis ipsa culpa; ipse naturæ reatus ex transgressione, sic quasi brutæ vitæ, quæ libidine ducatur, nec jam ratione, sed magis sensu vivat: ἀναίτιος vero, id est sine causa, quod laborem, cui succedat, ejusque causa sit, nullum habeat. Unde nec Christus sic ἀναίτιον nativitatem ex libidine assumpsit, quod non illo modo ἀναίτιος, sed illi comitem laborem, exque illa, ὡς αἰτίας, ut eo juste, cum in illo injustus esset, nullo scilicet in ipso reatu, illam aboleret. Quam belle cohæret, ut Maximo ἀδικωτάτῃ, injustissima, sit hæc voluptas seu libido, et tamen ipsa ἀναίτιος sit, ipsa sine culpa, bello interprete Pico? Nec enim ut labor injustus, sic et voluptas; quod hæc a voluntate exsistat, ille ab exteriore agente.
anchorLine: προκαθηγήσατο τῆς γενέσεως (p). Ἀναίτιον δέ φημι
en: "Ἀναιτίως προηγήσατο τῆς γενέσεως" (it went before birth without cause). Maximus guards, here and again in ch. 39, against taking anaitios and anaition as 'harmless' and 'without fault', which is the easy sense of the word, and which Picus eagerly adopts and renders everywhere. This pleasure is certainly not 'blameless' in that sense, but is joined to fault and arises from fault, if not itself the fault; it is nature's own liability from the transgression, as of a brute life led by lust and no longer by reason but rather by sense. 'Anaitios' properly means 'without cause', in that it has no labor following it and caused by it. So Christ did not take a birth from lust in that sense of 'anaition', but rather took labor as its companion, and by it, as by a cause, justly abolished the pleasure, since he was unjust in no way, having no liability in himself. How well it holds together, then, that for Maximus this pleasure or lust is 'most unjust' (adikotate), and yet is itself 'anaitios', itself without fault, as Picus handsomely translates! For pleasure is not unjust as labor is; this arises from the will, that from an external agent.

text: Οἱ μὲν τῇ φύσει. Quod sic hic, et sequenti cap. ac passim alibi Maximus naturam ingerit, ejusque rationem ut virtutis omnis regulam, ac necessitudinis cum Deo normam; ut tantum Deo uniamur ac virtute fulgeamus, simusque capaces æternæ beatitudinis, quantum nobis ac nostræ vo-

en: "Οἱ μὲν τῇ φύσει." That Maximus thus brings in nature here and in the next chapter, and often elsewhere, and its principle as the rule of all virtue and the norm of our relation with God, so that we are united to God and shine with virtue, and are capable of eternal blessedness, just so far as our own wil[l ...] (the note breaks off at the foot of the page and continues on p-0678).

text: [vo]luntati cum naturæ rationibus convenerit; de natura sanata et instituta per gratiam, omnino intelligendum non de ipsa quatenus in nobis ex transgressione pro peccato inolevit: de natura demum qualis a Deo condita fuit, imagine ornata et similitudine, in qua divini elucerent characteres, non cui obducta ex peccato brutorum ipsa πάθη (libidines scilicet), virtutis cultu ac exercitatione a nobis excutienda, ut divina in nobis instauretur vita, quod non aliter habemus, quam Christi gratia.
anchorLine: (continuation of note (r) from p-0677)
en: [...as far as] our will agrees with the principles of nature. Where nature healed and restored through grace is meant, it must be understood not of nature as it has grown up in us through the transgression as a result of sin, but of nature as it was created by God, adorned with the image and likeness in which divine characters shone; not of nature overlaid by sin with the brutish passions (that is, lusts), which must be shaken off by us through the practice and exercise of virtue, so that the divine life be restored in us, which we have in no other way than by the grace of Christ.

text: Τὸ ἓν ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῦ. Legit Picus ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ, ac reddere conatus est, Pie sub se habet unum, quod est et dicitur. Quod sane sensum habet absurdissimum, ac si velit Christum superius prædicatum esse, sub quo unum et sit et intelligatur. Ait itaque Maximus, unum pie semper in Christo et de Christo esse et intelligi, ea ratione qua persona est, nullamque distinctionem admittit. Deinde ὑπ᾽ αὐτὸν legendum foret, quod nec ipse repræsentat Picus.
anchorLine: κατὰ πάντα τρόπον τὸ ἓν ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῦ (s) διαπαντὸς
en: "Τὸ ἓν ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῦ." Picus read 'ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ' and tried to render it 'Piously he holds under himself one thing, which both is and is said', which makes an absurd sense, as if he meant that Christ had been predicated above, under whom the one both is and is understood. Maximus therefore says that the one is always piously in Christ and of Christ, and is understood [so], in the respect in which he is a person, and admits no distinction. Besides, 'ὑπ᾽ αὐτόν' would have had to be read, which Picus himself does not represent either.

text: Καὶ τὸν τῆς φύσεως νόμον. Legem naturæ toto hoc capite Maximus usurpat pro lege corporis, seu carnis et sensus, cum alias sæpe naturam, pro natura ipsa hominis qua homo est, ac ratione vivit atque virtute acceperit. Ubique sane in usu vo-
anchorLine: παραγενόμενος, καὶ τὸν τῆς φύσεως νόμον (t), ἤγουν
en: "Καὶ τὸν τῆς φύσεως νόμον." Throughout this chapter Maximus uses 'the law of nature' for the law of the body, that is, of the flesh and the senses, whereas elsewhere he often takes 'nature' for man's very nature as man, living by reason and virtue. In common usage indeed [the note breaks off at the foot of the page; it continues on p-0680].
